title: Spoken prompts with a multimodal model, and apps with Azure Speech
learningObjective: Respond to spoken prompts with a deployed multimodal model, and build a lightweight application with Azure Speech in Foundry Tools.
foundation: There are two ways to build a voice app. Option 1: Azure Speech turns speech into text, a model answers, and Azure Speech reads the answer aloud. Option 2: send the audio straight to a multimodal model that understands audio.
For live, natural conversations where the user can interrupt, use a real-time voice option (Voice Live or realtime models).
engineer: Azure Speech SDK (azure-cognitiveservices-speech): SpeechConfig (key or Entra token + endpoint/region); speech_recognition_language (for example en-US) or auto language detection; SpeechRecognizer with AudioConfig(use_default_microphone=True) or a filename; recognize_once_async().get() for one utterance; continuous recognition for long audio; check result.reason == ResultReason.RecognizedSpeech.

Text to speech: speech_config.speech_synthesis_voice_name = 'en-US-Ava:DragonHDLatestNeural'; SpeechSynthesizer(speech_config).speak_text_async(text).get(), or speak_ssml_async for SSML; output to speaker or file.

Multimodal audio input: deploy an audio-capable model; send the audio (base64, with its format) as an input content item alongside instructions; the model replies in text (or audio if supported). Good when tone and content both matter, with fewer moving parts.
Voice Live API / realtime: low-latency, bidirectional speech-to-speech for voice agents, with features such as noise suppression, turn detection and interruption handling.
Common errors: no microphone or wrong audio format, NoMatch (speech not recognised: check language), Canceled (check the cancellation details: auth, region/endpoint, quota).

animation.caption: Build a voice pipeline with Azure Speech or a multimodal model, and choose the approach for each requirement.

example.title: A hands-free warehouse assistant
body: Workers ask 'Where is pallet 4417?'. The app uses Azure Speech with a phrase list of product codes, sends the text to a model with a function to query the warehouse system, and speaks the answer with a neural voice.
A prototype that sends the recorded question directly to an audio-capable model needs fewer components but has less control over vocabulary.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription with access to Microsoft Foundry (ai.azure.com)
permissions: Azure AI User on the Foundry project to use models and agents; Azure AI Project Manager or Owner to create projects and deployments
limits: Model availability differs by region and deployment type
Deployments have tokens-per-minute (TPM) rate limits and quota per subscription and region
portal: Foundry portal > your project > Speech playground: try real-time speech to text and the voice gallery.
Language playground: run sentiment analysis and NER on sample text.
Copy the resource key and endpoint (or use Entra ID) from the resource's Keys and Endpoint page.

configuration.python:
# pip install azure-cognitiveservices-speech azure-ai-textanalytics
import os
import azure.cognitiveservices.speech as speechsdk
from azure.ai.textanalytics import TextAnalyticsClient
from azure.core.credentials import AzureKeyCredential

speech_config = speechsdk.SpeechConfig(subscription=os.environ["SPEECH_KEY"], endpoint=os.environ["ENDPOINT"])
speech_config.speech_recognition_language = "en-US"
recognizer = speechsdk.SpeechRecognizer(speech_config=speech_config,
                                        audio_config=speechsdk.audio.AudioConfig(use_default_microphone=True))
result = recognizer.recognize_once_async().get()
if result.reason == speechsdk.ResultReason.RecognizedSpeech:
    text = result.text
    language = TextAnalyticsClient(os.environ["ENDPOINT"], AzureKeyCredential(os.environ["SPEECH_KEY"]))
    sentiment = language.analyze_sentiment([text])[0]
    print(text, "->", sentiment.sentiment, sentiment.confidence_scores)

    speech_config.speech_synthesis_voice_name = "en-US-Ava:DragonHDLatestNeural"
    speechsdk.SpeechSynthesizer(speech_config=speech_config).speak_text_async(f"You sounded {sentiment.sentiment}.").get()
else:
    print("No speech recognized:", result.reason)
# Spoken prompt to an audio-capable model (openai = project.get_openai_client())
import base64
with open("question.wav", "rb") as f:
    audio_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()

completion = openai.chat.completions.create(
    model="audio-model",  # a deployment of an audio-capable model
    modalities=["text"],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "text", "text": "Answer the spoken question briefly."},
        {"type": "input_audio", "input_audio": {"data": audio_b64, "format": "wav"}},
    ]}],
)
print(completion.choices[0].message.content)

troubleshooting.cause: Speech didn't match the recognition language, or silence.
troubleshooting.fix: Set the correct language or use auto-detection; check the microphone.

troubleshooting.symptom: Result reason Canceled with an authentication error.
troubleshooting.cause: Wrong key, endpoint or region, or missing role.

comparisons.service: Speech SDK pipeline vs multimodal model
comparisons.difference: Pipeline: more control (custom speech, voices, SSML). Multimodal: simpler, understands audio directly.
Voice Live is real-time conversational; recognize_once handles one utterance.

misconceptions.myth: A multimodal model replaces all speech features.
misconceptions.reality: Custom speech, diarization and SSML still need Azure Speech.

architectureDecisions: Use Azure Speech when you need vocabulary control and specific voices.
Use multimodal audio for simple spoken Q&A.
Use Voice Live for natural real-time conversations.
